Upper-left view of female flower bud of Vallisneria circulating on the water. Trajectory of bud tip is shown in Fig. 1b. Upon reaching the water surface, bud displays pendulum-like circumnutation (stage 2). Thereafter, bud rotation is reinitiated and rotating bud circumnutates in a clockwise direction at 55.4 ± 8.0 min per rotation (stage 3). Next, circumnutation changes to a counter-clockwise direction at 45.9 ± 3.6 min per rotation and ratio of rotation/circumnutation is 0.90 ± 0.08 (stage 3). During circumnutation (5-17 h), irradiation intensity decreases from 15 to 8 µmol photons m −2 s −1 at the water surface. As peduncle elongates, circumnutation is reduced on the water surface (stage 4). Playback speed is 1,800×.

Movements of female flower bud and peduncle of Vallisneria underwater (stage 1), on water surface (stages 2-4), and coiling after pollination (stage 5). Images of this movie are shown in Fig. 1c. To observe stalk movement underwater, a silicone tube collar was attached near the bud base. In stage 1, stalk elongated by 0.72 ± 0.10 cm h −1 and time required for a single bud rotation is 5.3 h for the first rotation and gradually increases to 4.3 h, 4.0 h and 3.8 h for the second to the fourth from start of monitoring. Bud collar was removed after several circumnutations, but reflection on water surface shows rotational movement of bud and peduncle. Peduncle, (> 65 cm long) is compressed into a coil 20 cm in length beginning 36 h after pollination. Intensity of irradiation is 20 µmol photons m −2 s −1 at the water surface. Playback speed is 5,400×.

Movie 3. Simulating movement of Vallisneria female flowers using an artificial bud-peduncle model system. Images and trajectory of bud tip are shown in Fig. S3 and Fig.  5. Playback speed is 4×. In the first part of the movie, peduncle elongation without helical movement was simulated by draining water. In the second part, bud rotation without elongation was simulated by peduncle stirring. In both parts, there is no circumnutation. In the final part, the water was drained together with peduncle stirring. Experiment reproduced circumnutation on water surface.

Vallisneria asiatica var. biwaensis Miki in the field. (a) Growth of female flowers from base of water body to water surface by elongation of slender peduncles (water depth, 60 cm). (b) Floating female flowers on water surface. (c) Pollination of flowers on water surface. Mobile tiny male flowers aggregate around stigma of a female flower extending beyond the spathe (scale bar, 5 mm). Female flower consists of three sepals and three stigmas, each two-lobed and covered with papillose hairs. Ovary underwater is enclosed in a tubular spathe. Inset shows a male flower observed under a light microscope (scale bar, 0.5 mm). (d) Retraction of pollinated flowers underwater by tightly coiled peduncle. (e) Coiled peduncle of fruits underwater (scale bar, 10 cm). Asterisk: perversion. Pictures (a-d) were taken on the shore of Lake Biwa, Japan. Supplementary Figure S2. Continuous unidirectional helical growth of Vallisneria female flower peduncle in a deep-water tank. Flower bud showed ascending growth and rotation in a counter-clockwise direction. (a) Time required for a single bud rotation of two independent plants. Rotation speed gradually increased and was almost constant after 1-3 days. During the constant period, stalk elongated by 0.93 ± 0.30 cm h −1 and bud rotated 2.41 ± 0.58 h per rotation (n = 3). (b-e) Observation of basal intercalary growth of peduncle over time from start of monitoring. Seven silicone tube collars attached along peduncle (1-7) indicate that zone of intercalary growth is located near the base of the peduncle. Arrows indicate position of bud tip. Supplementary Figure S3. Simulated movements of Vallisneria female flowers using an artificial bud-peduncle model system. (a-d) Images recorded from Supplementary Movie 3.
